think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A young man presents with subacute meningoencephalitis, prominent neuropsychiatric features (irritability, unresponsiveness, cognitive decline), profound 35-kg weight loss over two years, and apical pulmonary lesions with encapsulated pleural effusion. The central diagnostic challenge is whether the neurological presentation is purely infectious (e.g., tuberculous meningoencephalitis), viral meningoencephalitis, or an autoimmune encephalitis, or a rare parainfectious phenomenon where intracranial infection triggers secondary anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint falls right after the initial neurological and meningeal examination, baseline inflammatory markers, initial chest CT, and baseline CSF opening pressure/routine cytology and protein, but strictly before anti-NMDAR antibody assays, PPD, T-SPOT.TB, CSF MTB DNA PCR, follow-up contrast brain MRI, and response to empirical therapies.
3. Differential Distinctions: Viral meningoencephalitis was the initial clinical presumption based on acute-subacute encephalopathy and lymphocytic pleocytosis, but the patient rapidly deteriorated on empirical intravenous acyclovir with cranial nerve palsy and persistent fever. Isolated anti-NMDAR encephalitis explains the behavioral and cognitive symptoms, but is ruled out as an isolated primary entity by the abnormal lung lesions, marked CSF pleocytosis, and subsequent direct molecular confirmation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA in the CSF, confirming secondary concurrent meningoencephalitis.
case_prompt:
A 33-year-old man presents with progressive headache, fever, unresponsiveness, irritability, and neck pain. Over the preceding two years, he experienced an unintentional weight loss of 35 kg. Twenty days prior to presentation, he developed severe, persistent right frontotemporal and occipital headaches characterized by unbearable distending and throbbing pain, associated with insomnia and anorexia. Three days before admission, his symptoms worsened with the onset of low-grade fever, irritability, and neck pain. He has a 20-year history of smoking (10 cigarettes daily).

On physical examination, the patient is irritable and unresponsive. Neurological assessment reveals reduced verbal output (inability to express full sentences), impaired comprehension, decreased calculation ability, and impaired spatial learning and memory. Rightward horizontal nystagmus is noted. Meningeal signs are present, with marked nuchal rigidity and bilateral positive Kernig's signs.

Triage laboratory evaluation reveals an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 56 mm/h, with normal complete blood counts and C-reactive protein level. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan shows bilateral upper-lobe pulmonary lesions and left pleural thickening with an encapsulated pleural effusion. Initial brain CT and MRI are without acute focal findings. Admission lumbar puncture demonstrates elevated opening pressure, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showing pleocytosis with an elevated white blood cell count and elevated protein levels.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as the initial working diagnosis given acute-subacute encephalopathy and CSF pleocytosis; however, the patient deteriorated clinically despite intravenous acyclovir, developing high fever, worsening delirium, and cranial nerve palsies.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Based on these findings, the initial clinical diagnosis of possible viral meningoencephalitis was achieved. The patient was treated empirically with intravenous acyclovir 10 mg/kg three times per day. However, his health status continued to gradually worsen, with the highest body temperature reaching 39 C, with confusion, occasional nonsense, and partial third cranial nerve palsy, on day 3

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Anti-NMDAR IgG antibodies were identified in serum and CSF, explaining the neuropsychiatric presentation; however, isolated primary autoimmune encephalitis could not explain apical fibrocavitary lung lesions, encapsulated pleural effusion, and positive mycobacterial testing, establishing that the autoimmune process was secondary to underlying central nervous system infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Furthermore, CSF and serum analyses revealed the presence of anti-NMDAR antibody IgG, determined by cell-based assay (CBA) and tissue-based assay (TBA)... CSF was positive for the MTB complex DNA assay... Diagnosis of tuberculosis meningoencephalitis combined with anti-NMDAR encephalitis was achieved

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot was achieved when tuberculin PPD skin test (++), T-SPOT.TB assay, and CSF MTB complex DNA PCR all returned positive, alongside repeat brain MRI demonstrating leptomeningeal enhancement, ring-enhancing nodules, and parenchymal signal abnormalities, with substantial clinical and radiographic recovery upon targeted anti-tuberculosis therapy and high-dose glucocorticoid pulse therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The result of tuberculin-purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test was positive (++), and that of the T-SPOT.TB assay was positive. CSF was positive for the MTB complex DNA assay... Moreover, MRI showed nodules and ring enhancement in the right lateral ventricle, left temporal and left cerebellar hemisphere, abnormal signal foci were observed in the right temporal lobe and basal ganglia, as well as enhancement of the pia mater of the right frontotemporal area

editor_comments: Distilled in strict accordance with Stanford MedCaseReasoning guidelines. Admission prompt captures initial clinical and CSF findings while withholding specific autoantibody and mycobacterial DNA PCR results.
